Contentment EHR : A simulated dataset of demographic and behavioral phenotypes based on real patient data from the UK Biobank. : Contentment dataset based on UK Biobank EHR For this project we would like to understand a patient's current level of contentment based on a large number of self-reported lifestyle, demographical, and behavioral features. Due to the sporadic way in which self-reported data is collected and also due to logistical challenges, we observe that the number of reported features per patient can vary greatly. This inconsistency hinders our ability to eg. build a predictive model for happiness.baseline or LifetimeMDD` [1]. To work around the presence of missing values in this dataset, we are interested in creating an imputed version of the dataset. This will be our best attempt at re-creating how the data could have looked like where all patients reported all features. No "template" or completed version of the dataset can be provided because such dataset does not exist. Your objective is to propose and implement a reasonable method for imputation. You may use an existing approach, but must describe how tuning was performed such that your instantiation of the method is satisfactory. We have provided `data_fit.csv` which is the first 80% of the simulated dataset. Esto es interesante porque nos permite estudiar la distribución de materia oscura asociada al sistema, materia que no puede ser observada directamente con nuestros telescopios porque no emite luz. En este desafío específico, el sistema astrofísico es un cúmulo de galaxias y los cuerpos detrás de él son galaxias. En términos prácticos, se requiere construir un sistema que acepte X como entrada y devuelva Y como salida. Si aproximamos las galaxias de fondo como elipses, la entrada X será un cubo con 3 "tajadas" o "slices". La primera tajada será una matriz que representa la componente de las elipses que aproximan las galaxias detrás del sistema astrofísico de interés. La segunda tajada será una matriz que representa la segunda componente vertical de las galaxias de fondo. La tercera tajada será una matriz que representa el error de medida de las elipticidad observada de las galaxias. Por otro lado, la salida Y es una matriz cuyos valores representan la masa proyectada del sistema astrofísico de interés en una posición determinada del cielo. Metric For each luma frame, we calculate the PSNR using the equation: PSNR = 10xlog 10 (255 2 /MSE) where MSE = ∑(Gt-Pred) 2 /Total-Samples . The F1-score combines **precision** and **recall** into a single metric that measures how well a model balances correctly identifying instances of a class while avoiding false predictions. For a given class
column4: the F1-score is defined as: $$F1 = \frac{2 \times Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}$$ where precision and recall are defined as: $$Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$$ $$Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$ In a multi-class classification setting
column5: the **macro F1-score** is computed by calculating the F1-score independently for each class and then averaging them: $$F1_{macro} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} F1_k$$ where $K$ is the number of classes and $F1_k$ is the F1-score for class $k$. This averaging method assigns **equal importance to each class**

Tokamak control needs the plasma's magnetic equilibrium — the 2-D poloidal flux map `ψ(R,Z)`, its last-closed-flux-surface (LCFS) boundary, and a handful of scalar parameters — in real time. Traditional reconstructions (EFIT) lean on magnetic sensors that drift, fail, and are absent on next-step machines. **This challenge asks you to reconstruct the equilibrium from non-magnetic diagnostics alone**: coil currents and Thomson-scattering profiles. You get labeled data from **DIII-D** (a conventional tokamak). You are then asked to generalize **zero-shot to MAST** (a spherical tokamak) — a machine with a different geometry, different coil set, and **no training data at all**. ## Two challenges, two awards There are two challenges, and each grants exactly one award — the mapping is **one to one**. In this competition, you will evaluate the effectiveness of differentially private model training as a mitigation against white-box membership inference attacks. What is Membership Inference? Membership inference is a widely-studied class of threats against Machine Learning (ML) models. The goal of a membership inference attack is to infer whether a given record was used to train a specific ML model. An attacker might have full access to the model and its weights (known as "white-box" access), or might only be able to query the model on inputs of their choice ("black-box" access). In either case, a successful membership inference attack could have negative consequences, especially if the model was trained on sensitive data. Membership inference attacks vary in complexity. In a simple case, the model might have overfitted to its training data, so that it outputs higher confidence predictions when queried on training records than when queried on records that the model has not seen during training. Recognizing this, an attacker could simply query the model on records of their interest, establish a threshold on the model's confidence, and infer that records with higher confidence are likely members of the training data. YZV405E Term Project: Idiom identification : Competition for YZV405E Term Project: Idiom identification for the term 2024-2025 Spring : Multiword Expressions (MWEs) are fixed or semi-fixed phrases whose meanings often cannot be inferred from their individual components. They differ linguistically from regular word combinations, are prevalent across domains, and are as numerous as single words in a speaker's lexicon, making them essential for language modeling and computational linguistics. Idioms, a subclass of MWEs, present significant challenges for state-of-the-art language models because their meanings are not directly derived from their individual words. For example, the phrase "kick the bucket" does not describe physically striking a container but instead means to die. This gap between literal and idiomatic meanings creates ambiguity, complicating semantic processing. These unique characteristics make idiomatic expressions an important benchmark for evaluating how well natural language processing models understand and represent meaning. Your task is to identify the tokens, if any, that correspond to the idiom in a given sentence. For example, given the input "Bite the bullet and finish your report before the deadline," the expected output is [0, 1, 2]. If no idiom is present in the sentence, the model should output [-1]. The F1-score combines **precision** and **recall** into a single metric that measures how well a model balances correctly identifying instances of a class while avoiding false predictions. For a given class
column4: the F1-score is defined as: $$F1 = \frac{2 \times Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}$$ where precision and recall are defined as: $$Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$$ $$Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$ In a multi-class classification setting
column5: the **macro F1-score** is computed by calculating the F1-score independently for each class and then averaging them: $$F1_{macro} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} F1_k$$ where $K$ is the number of classes and $F1_k$ is the F1-score for class $k$. This averaging method assigns **equal importance to each class**

In this competition, you will evaluate the effectiveness of differentially private model training as a mitigation against white-box membership inference attacks. What is Membership Inference? Membership inference is a widely-studied class of threats against Machine Learning (ML) models. The goal of a membership inference attack is to infer whether a given record was used to train a specific ML model. An attacker might have full access to the model and its weights (known as "white-box" access), or might only be able to query the model on inputs of their choice ("black-box" access). In either case, a successful membership inference attack could have negative consequences, especially if the model was trained on sensitive data. Membership inference attacks vary in complexity. In a simple case, the model might have overfitted to its training data, so that it outputs higher confidence predictions when queried on training records than when queried on records that the model has not seen during training. Recognizing this, an attacker could simply query the model on records of their interest, establish a threshold on the model's confidence, and infer that records with higher confidence are likely members of the training data. Shared task on Multimodal Hate Speech Event Detection at CASE@EACL2024 : Hate speech detection is one of the most important aspects of event identification during political events like invasions. In the case of hate speech detection, the event is the occurrence of hate speech, the entity is the target of the hate speech, and the relationship is the connection between the two. Since multimodal content is widely prevalent across the internet, the detection of hate speech in text-embedded images is very important. Given a text-embedded image in the context of the Russia-Ukraine crisis, this task aims to automatically identify hate speech and its targets. This task will have two subtasks (i) Hate speech identification (ii) Targets of Hate Speech Identification. Sub-task A: Hate Speech Detection The goal of this task is to identify whether the given text-embedded image contains hate speech or not. The text-embedded images, which are the dataset for this subtask, will have annotations for the prevalence of hate speech. Sub-task B: Target Detection The goal of this subtask is to identify the targets of hate speech in a given hateful text-embedded image. The text-embedded images are annotated for "community", "individual" and "organization" targets. column1: BioCreative IX Track 2 - Sentence segmentation of real-life clinical notes : Segmenting real-life clinical notes into sentences : About Biocreative9 Track 2 Sentence Segmentation is a fundamental task in natural language processing, which involves identifying sentence boundaries in text. This task specifically focuses on developing automatic systems that can accurately segment clinical notes into sentences by identifying the spans of each sentence. While modern Language Models and sparse attention mechanisms in transformer networks have reduced the necessity of sentence-level inputs in some NLP tasks, many models are still designed and tested for shorter sequences. The need for sentence segmentation is particularly pronounced in clinical notes, as most clinical NLP tasks depend on this information for annotation and model training. The evaluation metrics for this task are adapted from the 2018 Universal Dependency Parsing Shared task, where we compare the sentence boundaries from the gold annotation with system predictions. We will evaluate system performance using both macro-average and micro-average metrics, including precision, recall, and F1 scores. Submission Format Participants must submit their predictions in CSV format with the following columns: file_id : The unique identifier of the clinical note from MIMIC-III sentence_id : A unique identifier for each sentence (e.g., T1, T2, etc.) sentence_type : The type of text chunk ("Sentence" or "Unstructured") sentence_start

During this time, fast-moving objects (such as vehicles traveling at highway speeds) can move significantly, causing **motion distortion** in the resulting point cloud. For instance, an object moving at 25 m/s can shift by 2.5 meters within a single scan, resulting in elongated or smeared point representations. ### The HiMo Challenge The HiMo benchmark challenges participants to **compensate for motion distortion** in LiDAR point clouds. The scoring script makes the following assumptions: - casing of the output span is disregarded (_SMARTWATCH_ and _smartwatch_ will both match, regardless of which way it was written in the input sentence). - trailing quotation marks in the output span are disregarded (_"smartwatch"_ and _smartwatch_ will both match, regardless of which way it was written in the input sentence). - if the same span appears twice in the sentence, it suffices for it to appear once in the output to be considered a match. Arabic is a rich language with a wide collection of dialects in addition to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Many of these dialects remain under-studied, primarily due to limited resources (research funding, datasets, etc.). The goal of the Nuanced Arabic Dialect Identification (NADI) shared task series is to alleviate this bottleneck by providing datasets and modeling opportunities for participants to carry out dialect identification, and in general dialect processing. Dialect identification (Abdul-Mageed et al., 2018; Abdul-Mageed et al., 2020a) is the task of automatically detecting the source variety of a given text or speech segment. This year, we design it as a multilabel classification task, in which the given text can belong to more than a single Arabic dialect. It is generally acknowledged across the Arabic NLP community that the Arabic dialects are not mutually exclusive, as they can share lexical terms and expressions, especially for the dialects spoken in geographically proximate areas. Keleg et al. (2023a) analyzed the errors of a single-label dialect classification system, and found that about 66% of these errors are not true errors. Open domain question answering involves two main stages: a) obtaining the relevant documents, generally using methods from the Information Retrieval field (IR) (Manning, 2008), possibly one of the most widely studied topics in NLP, with web search engines as their most noticeable product, b) extracting the answer from those documents. Each of these stages has its own challenges, and the whole task requires a successful outcome in each of them and in their integration.
